title: Roles, scopes and tenants: write can()
prompt:
In the reading app, a district contains schools, which contain classes. People get a role at one level of that tree: a teacher is granted teacher on one class, a principal on one school, a district admin on a whole district. Students submit work.

The starter's can() checks only the role and ignores where it was granted. Run the tests to see what that leaks. Then implement can(user, action, resource) so that it returns true only when some grant of the user satisfies all of:

  1. Permission: PERMISSIONS[grant.role] includes resource.type + ':' + action (e.g. 'submission:grade').
  2. Scope: every key in grant.scope equals the same key on the resource. A grant on { districtId: 'd1', schoolId: 's1' } covers every class in school s1 of district d1. An empty or missing scope covers nothing.
  3. Ownership: a student grant only covers submissions whose ownerId is the user's own id.

Anything not explicitly allowed is denied: unknown roles, unknown actions, users with no grants.

const resource = { type: 'submission', districtId: 'd1', schoolId: 's1', classId: 'c1', ownerId: 'u-ana' };
can(msLee, 'grade', resource);   // true: teacher of c1
can(ana,   'read',  resource);   // true: her own work
can(ben,   'read',  resource);   // false: classmate's work

tests.name: a teacher can read and grade submissions in their own class
a teacher cannot grade in another class, even in the same school
a principal covers every class in their school, and only their school
tenant isolation: a district admin never reaches another district
students see their own submissions, not their classmates'
several grants: any one that fully matches is enough
deny by default: no grants, unknown roles, unknown actions, empty scopes

hints: Keep the starter's permission check, and add two more conditions inside the same some(). A grant only counts if it passes all three: what (permission), where (scope), whose (ownership for students).
Scope check: Object.keys(g.scope).every(k => resource[k] === g.scope[k]). Careful: [].every(...) is true, so an empty scope would match everything. Treat zero keys as "covers nothing".

The shape:

return user.grants.some((g) => {
  if (!(PERMISSIONS[g.role] || []).includes(perm)) return false;
  if (!covers(g.scope, resource)) return false;
  if (g.role === 'student' && resource.type === 'submission')
    return resource.ownerId === user.id;
  return true;
});
explain:
You just wrote the core of most B2B authorization: role-based access control (RBAC) with scoped grants, plus one attribute rule (ownership). Tools like Google Zanzibar, OpenFGA, Oso and Cerbos generalize exactly this: who has which relation to which node of a tree, and rules that walk the tree.

The bug in the starter is the most common authorization bug in real products. The check asks "is this person a teacher?" when it should ask "is this person a teacher of this class?". Combined with guessable IDs in URLs, that is an IDOR (insecure direct object reference): change /classes/c1 to /classes/c3 and see another school's data. In edtech that's student data, which is also a legal problem (FERPA, COPPA).

Say it: "Every request resolves the tenant from the session, not from the URL. Authorization is one function, can(user, action, resource), called in every handler and backed by scoped role grants. It fails closed. As a second line of defense, every query is filtered by district_id, and in Postgres I'd add row-level security so a forgotten WHERE clause can't leak another district's data."
